Distinguished participants, 35 years ago, on 29th August 1991, Kazakhstan took a decision that would become a defining moment in the country's history and an important milestone in the global struggle against nuclear testing. By presidential decree, Kazakhstan permanently closed the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, one of the largest nuclear test sites in the world. For more than four decades, 456 nuclear tests were conducted at the Semipalatinsk test site, 30 atmospheric, 86 above ground, and 340 underground nuclear explosions. And behind every number of explosions are people who suffered from nuclear tests, families, communities, children yet to be born. The closure of the Semipalatinsk test site was the result of the strong determination and will of the people of Kazakhstan. In 1989, the first major anti-nuclear movement in Kazakhstan emerged, under the leadership of the renowned Kazakh poet and activist, Olzhas Zhuliyenov. The Semipalatinsk Nevada anti-nuclear movement called for the closure of the test site and demonstrated that ordinary people, when united by a common cause, can influence the course of history. Its name reflected solidarity with similar movements in the United States. that sought an end to nuclear testing at the Nevada Test Site. Pursuant to a United Nations General Assembly resolution initiated by Kazakhstan in 2009, 29 August is observed as the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. The day serves to raise awareness of the devastating consequences of nuclear testing and to strengthen international efforts towards its prohibition. This experience became part of Kazakhstan's enduring commitment to nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and the prohibition of nuclear testing. Distinguished participants, the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 have become one of the greatest tragedies in human history. The humanitarian and environmental consequences of nuclear testing in Kazakhstan were catastrophic. The Semipalatinsk test site covered 18,000 square kilometers, an area profoundly affected by radioactive contamination. Approximately 1.5 million people were exposed to high levels of radiation, with consequences that have continued to affect generations. The impact has been felt through increased health problems, congenital birth defects, and the long-term psychological and social consequences of living with the legacy of nuclear testing. The environmental consequences have also been profound. Contamination of soil, restrictions on land use, the need for long-term monitoring of radioactive pathways through water, and the continuing risk of radioactive particles being transported by wind and entering the food chain through plants and animals. From the first days of its independence, Kazakhstan therefore took concrete steps to address this legacy. Within the framework of the Cooperative Threat Reduction Program, Kazakhstan, together with the United States and the Russian Federation, dismantled and eliminated all the military infrastructure of the nuclear test site. Based on scientific facilities of the testing site, Kazakhstan has established National Nuclear Center, the world-class scientific and technological complex, working now to advance international security and the peaceful uses of nuclear energy. The center conducted comprehensive environmental assessments, alongside remediation and other measures to address the consequences of nuclear testing. In 1992, Kazakhstan adopted the law on social protection of citizens who suffered from nuclear tests at the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site. And the government of Kazakhstan continues to provide direct support to affected populations. Since 1997, the United Nations General Assembly has adopted resolutions entitled International Cooperation and Coordination for the Human and Ecological Rehabilitation and Economic Development of the Semipalatinsk Region of Kazakhstan, calling for continued international cooperation. We remain grateful to all countries and international organizations that have supported Kazakhstan in overcoming this difficult legacy.
